metaDescription: Printable beginner knee osteoarthritis exercises, also called knee arthritis exercises, with strength, walking, symptom rules, and clear progression.
kicker: Knee osteoarthritis · Beginner home exercise plan
h1: Beginner Knee Osteoarthritis Exercises
summary: Exercise is a foundational treatment for knee osteoarthritis. This beginner plan builds strength for walking, stairs, and chair transfers with a practical dose and a next-morning symptom rule.

authorityItems.text: Five practical movements for daily function
Strength plus walking or cycling
A six-week checkpoint, then long-term maintenance

fitIntro: This beginner program is intended for adults who have already been evaluated and told knee osteoarthritis is the likely diagnosis. It is not a self-diagnosis tool, a postoperative protocol, or a substitute for individualized care.
fit: Activity-related knee pain and stiffness, often in adults over 45, with difficulty during walking, stairs, rising from a chair, or prolonged activity.
assessFirst: Recent major injury, a diagnosis that is uncertain, substantial instability, inflammatory arthritis, recent surgery, or pain that is mainly coming from the hip, back, or nerves.
redFlags: Call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or another medical emergency. Seek same-day urgent assessment for a new or rapidly worsening painful, hot, red, or swollen joint with or without fever, new one-sided calf swelling, inability to bear weight after trauma, true locking, or rapid deformity. Arrange a prompt evaluation for unexplained persistent rest or night pain.
programHeading: Build a base for daily life.
programIntro: No single exercise mode or dose is best for everyone. Start with one set if needed, use a range that keeps movement controlled, then build repetitions, sets, resistance, range, or time gradually.
frequency: Strength 2 to 3 days per week; aerobic activity on most days
equipment: Stable chair, low step, optional band or backpack
checkpoint: Reassess function after 6 weeks
goal: Easier walking, stairs, and chair transfers

exercises.name: Sit to stand
exercises.how: Sit near the front of a stable chair. Lean your chest slightly forward, press through both feet, stand tall, then lower with control.
exercises.easier: Use a higher chair or push lightly from the armrests.
exercises.harder: Lower the chair or hold a light backpack at your chest.

exercises.name: Low step-up
exercises.dose: 1 to 3 sets of 5 to 10 repetitions per side
exercises.how: Place one foot on a low step. Keep the knee tracking over the middle toes, rise onto the step, then lower slowly. Use a rail for balance.
exercises.easier: Use a shorter step and more hand support.
exercises.harder: Use a taller step or hold a light weight.

exercises.name: Bridge
exercises.how: Lie on your back with knees bent. Gently brace your abdomen, press through the heels, lift the hips until the body forms a comfortable line, then lower slowly.
exercises.easier: Lift through a smaller range.
exercises.harder: Add a band above the knees or use a staggered foot position.

exercises.name: Seated knee extension
exercises.dose: 1 to 3 sets of 8 to 15 repetitions per side
exercises.how: Sit tall. Slowly straighten one knee, pause with the thigh supported, then lower with control. Keep the movement smooth rather than snapping the knee straight.
exercises.easier: Use a smaller range or fewer repetitions.
exercises.harder: Add a light ankle weight or resistance band.

exercises.name: Walking or cycling base
exercises.how: Choose walking, stationary cycling, swimming, or another rhythmic activity that you can repeat consistently. A shorter session still counts.
exercises.easier: Use two shorter sessions or choose a lower-impact option.
exercises.harder: Add 2 to 5 minutes per week before adding speed or hills.

responseIntro: Mild to moderate discomfort can be acceptable when movement stays controlled and symptoms return to your usual baseline by the next day.
green: Mild discomfort, no new limp, and the knee is back to its usual baseline by the following morning.
yellow: Pain, swelling, or limping is meaningfully worse later that day or remains worse the next morning. Reduce depth, load, repetitions, or aerobic time.
red: Stop. Call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or another medical emergency. Seek same-day urgent assessment for a new or rapidly worsening painful, hot, red, or swollen joint with or without fever, new one-sided calf swelling, true locking, rapidly increasing swelling, or inability to bear weight after trauma.

progression.title: Stage 1: establish tolerance
progression.text: Use a comfortable range and the lower end of each repetition range. Prioritize smooth movement and symptoms that return to baseline by the next day.

progression.title: Stage 2: build strength
progression.text: Reach the top of the repetition range, then lower the chair, raise the step, add a band or backpack, or slow the lowering phase.

progression.title: Stage 3: decide whether to advance
progression.text: Increase walking or cycling time and practice the activities you want to regain. Consider the advanced program when the full beginner dose is controlled and your goals require more strength for stairs, hills, carrying, or recreation.

readyItems: The current dose feels controlled for several sessions.
Symptoms return to baseline by the next morning.
You can complete the upper repetition range with controlled movement.
Your goals require more strength for stairs, hills, carrying, or recreation.
evaluation: Schedule a visit if symptoms are worsening, daily function has not improved after about six weeks, swelling repeatedly limits exercise, or you need help distinguishing arthritis from another knee problem.

faqs.q: Should I avoid exercise because the knee is worn down?
faqs.a: No. Appropriately dosed exercise has not been shown to accelerate knee osteoarthritis. Progressive strength and aerobic activity are core treatments and can improve pain, function, and confidence.

faqs.q: Which exercise is best for knee arthritis?
faqs.a: No single mode is universally superior. Strength, aerobic activity, and mobility can all help. The best plan is one you can perform consistently and progress without a sustained symptom flare.

faqs.q: Can I exercise when the knee hurts?
faqs.a: Some discomfort can be acceptable. Use the next-day response: if pain, swelling, or limping remains meaningfully worse the following morning, reduce the dose.

faqs.q: How long should I continue?
faqs.a: Use six to twelve weeks to build the habit and assess progress, then continue the useful elements long term. Benefits are maintained through ongoing activity.

faqs.q: When should I move to the advanced program?
faqs.a: Consider advancing when you can complete this program at the intended dose with controlled movement, your knee returns to its usual baseline by the next morning, and your goals require greater strength or endurance. Advanced refers to exercise complexity, not arthritis severity.

metaDescription: Printable advanced knee osteoarthritis exercises for strength, stairs, hills, balance, aerobic conditioning, symptom rules, and progression.
kicker: Knee osteoarthritis · Advanced home exercise plan
h1: Advanced Knee Osteoarthritis Exercises
summary: This progression is for people who tolerate the beginner program and want greater strength, single-leg control, and aerobic capacity for higher-demand daily or recreational activity.

authorityItems.text: Progressive resistance for higher strength demands
Single-leg control for stairs, hills, and uneven ground
A next-morning rule that guides progression

fitIntro: This advanced exercise program is intended for adults with an established knee osteoarthritis diagnosis who tolerate the beginner program and want more capacity for demanding daily or recreational activity. Advanced describes exercise complexity, not X-ray severity.
fit: Stable next-day symptoms with the beginner program and goals such as climbing stairs and hills more easily, carrying, hiking, travel, or recreation.
assessFirst: Frequent swelling, repeated giving way or falls, inability to tolerate the beginner plan, a recent major injury or surgery, an uncertain diagnosis, or medical conditions that may require an individualized exercise prescription.
redFlags: Call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or another medical emergency. Seek same-day urgent assessment for a new or rapidly worsening painful, hot, red, or swollen joint with or without fever, new one-sided calf swelling, inability to bear weight after trauma, true locking, or rapid deformity. Arrange a prompt evaluation for unexplained persistent rest or night pain.
programHeading: Progress the demand, not the flare.
programIntro: No exercise intensity or mode is proven best for every person with knee osteoarthritis. Advanced does not mean maximal effort. Stop each set while you could still complete two or three controlled repetitions, progress one variable at a time, and use the next-morning response to judge the total dose.
frequency: Strength 2 to 3 nonconsecutive days per week; aerobic activity 3 to 5 days per week
equipment: Stable chair, step, resistance band, and dumbbell or loaded backpack
checkpoint: Reassess strength and function after 6 to 8 weeks
goal: Greater capacity for stairs, hills, carrying, hiking, and recreation

exercises.name: Loaded squat to a chair
exercises.how: Hold a dumbbell or loaded backpack close to your chest. Sit the hips back toward a stable chair, keep both feet grounded, then stand tall with controlled knee alignment.
exercises.easier: Use a higher chair, lighter load, or smaller range.
exercises.harder: Add a small amount of weight or lower the chair after the upper repetition range feels controlled.

exercises.name: Supported split squat
exercises.dose: 2 to 3 sets of 6 to 10 repetitions per side
exercises.how: Stand in a staggered stance beside a stable support. Lower both knees through a comfortable range while keeping the front foot planted, then push through the front leg to rise.
exercises.easier: Use more hand support, a shorter stance, or a smaller range.
exercises.harder: Use less support, increase the range, or hold light weight.

exercises.name: Step-up with controlled step-down
exercises.dose: 2 to 3 sets of 6 to 10 repetitions per side
exercises.how: Step onto a stable step, stand fully, then lower over three seconds without dropping the pelvis or letting the knee collapse inward. Keep a rail within reach.
exercises.easier: Use a shorter step, fingertip support, or a smaller range.
exercises.harder: Add light weight or increase step height one level at a time.

exercises.name: Resisted knee extension
exercises.dose: 2 to 4 sets of 8 to 15 repetitions per side
exercises.how: Anchor a resistance band behind the chair or use an ankle weight. Straighten one knee smoothly, pause, then lower over two to three seconds while the thigh stays supported.
exercises.easier: Use lighter resistance or a smaller comfortable range.
exercises.harder: Increase resistance gradually after 15 controlled repetitions.

exercises.name: Supported single-leg hip hinge
exercises.dose: 2 to 3 sets of 6 to 10 repetitions per side
exercises.how: Stand beside a stable support with most of your weight on one leg. Keep a soft knee, hinge the trunk forward from the hip, then press through the standing foot and tighten the gluteal muscles to return upright without twisting.
exercises.easier: Keep the back toes on the floor as a kickstand and use hand support.
exercises.harder: Lift the back foot, reduce hand support, or hold a light weight.

exercises.name: Aerobic capacity progression
exercises.how: Choose walking, cycling, swimming, or another repeatable activity. Build total time first. When the next-morning response is stable, one session can include short brisk intervals or gentle hills.
exercises.easier: Use 10 to 20 continuous minutes, split the session, or choose cycling or pool exercise.
exercises.harder: Add one interval, a small hill, or 2 to 5 minutes, but not all three at once.

responseIntro: Mild to moderate discomfort can be acceptable when technique remains controlled and pain, swelling, limping, and function return to your usual baseline by the next morning.
green: Mild discomfort, steady movement quality, no new limp, and the knee is back to its usual baseline by the following morning.
yellow: Pain, swelling, limping, or stair function is meaningfully worse later that day or remains worse the next morning. Reduce load, range, repetitions, step height, or aerobic time.
red: Stop. Call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or another medical emergency. Seek same-day urgent assessment for a new or rapidly worsening painful, hot, red, or swollen joint with or without fever, new one-sided calf swelling, true locking, rapidly increasing swelling, or inability to bear weight after trauma.

progression.title: Stage 1: practice the movements with control
progression.text: Start at the lower dose with support and a comfortable range. Stop each set while you could still complete two or three controlled repetitions rather than training to failure.

progression.title: Stage 2: add one strength variable
progression.text: First reach the upper repetition range. Then add a small amount of resistance, range, step height, or single-leg demand while the next-morning response stays stable.

progression.title: Stage 3: train the goal
progression.text: Gradually practice the stairs, hills, carrying tasks, walking duration, or recreational activities you want to improve. Increase only one demand at a time so you can interpret the response.

readyItems: The current load and range feel controlled for several sessions.
Symptoms return to baseline by the next morning.
You can perform the task on both sides without a new limp or loss of balance.
You can increase one variable without swelling or a meaningful loss of next-day function.
evaluation: Schedule a visit if symptoms are worsening, swelling repeatedly limits progression, the knee locks or gives way, daily function has not improved after six to eight weeks, or you need an individualized plan for a higher-risk medical condition or sport goal.

faqs.q: Does advanced mean my arthritis is severe?
faqs.a: No. Advanced describes the exercise challenge, not X-ray grade or disease severity. A person with substantial X-ray changes may need a beginner plan, while someone with milder changes may tolerate more complex loading.

faqs.q: Is heavier exercise better for knee pain?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. High-intensity strength training has not shown better knee-pain outcomes than lower-intensity training. Use enough resistance to build capacity while preserving control and returning to your usual symptom baseline by the next day.

faqs.q: Should I train through swelling?
faqs.a: No. A small, brief symptom increase may be acceptable, but meaningful or persistent swelling is a sign to reduce the dose and consider an evaluation if it keeps returning.

faqs.q: Do I need to do all six exercises every session?
faqs.a: No. Two or three strength sessions can divide the movements across the week. Consistency and progressive exposure matter more than completing every exercise in one session.

faqs.q: Do I need jumping or running in an advanced arthritis program?
faqs.a: No. Impact exercise is optional and should match your goals, examination, history, and tolerance. Strong walking, stairs, cycling, hiking, and resistance training are meaningful advanced goals without jumping.

title: Patellofemoral Pain Home Exercise Program

video.title: Patellofemoral Pain | Chondromalacia Patellae | Runner’s Knee (Education | Myths | Exercises)
video.description: A visual overview of patellofemoral pain, load management, and common hip and knee exercise progressions.
video.caution: The examples include later, higher-stress options. Do not add them all or jump directly to deeper or higher-volume versions. Follow this page’s pain limit, next-morning rule, and three-day strength dose.

metaDescription: Printable patellofemoral pain exercises for front-of-knee pain, with hip and knee strengthening, symptom rules, and clear progression.
kicker: Front-of-knee pain · Home exercise plan
h1: Patellofemoral Pain Exercises
summary: Patellofemoral pain care should pair education with progressive knee-targeted exercise. Hip-targeted exercise can be added when it matches symptoms, impairments, preferences, or early knee-loading tolerance.
authorityTitle: Knee strength. Hip strength. Load control.

authorityItems.text: Knee-targeted strengthening, with hip exercise when indicated
Progressive exposure to squatting and stairs
Workload changes matched to your symptoms

fitIntro: This starter program is intended for adults who have already been evaluated and told patellofemoral pain is the likely diagnosis. It is not a self-diagnosis tool, a postoperative protocol, or a substitute for individualized care.
fit: Pain around or behind the kneecap that is reproduced by squatting, stairs, running, jumping, or prolonged sitting.
assessFirst: A recent traumatic injury, major swelling, recurrent kneecap dislocation, pain focused at the patellar tendon or tibial tubercle, or pain that is not reproduced by loaded knee bending.
redFlags: Call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or another medical emergency. Seek same-day urgent assessment for traumatic swelling, inability to bear weight, true locking, loss of knee extension, a kneecap dislocation, rapidly worsening pain, or a new painful, hot, red, or swollen joint with or without fever.
programHeading: Share the work across the knee and hip.
programIntro: Begin with more hip-focused work when loaded knee bending is especially painful. As tolerance improves, gradually restore knee range, repetitions, step height, and resistance.
frequency: 3 nonconsecutive strength days per week
equipment: Stable chair, low step, optional loop band
checkpoint: Look for improvement by 6 to 8 weeks
goal: More comfortable squatting, stairs, running, and sitting

exercises.name: Sit to stand or shallow squat
exercises.how: Use a chair as a target. Keep the feet grounded, knees tracking over the middle toes, and lower only as far as you can control.
exercises.easier: Use a higher chair or a shallower squat.
exercises.harder: Lower the chair, deepen the squat gradually, or hold light weight.

exercises.name: Low step-down
exercises.dose: 3 sets of 6 to 12 repetitions per side
exercises.how: Stand on a low step with support nearby. Bend the standing knee slowly as the opposite heel reaches toward the floor, then return without the knee collapsing inward.
exercises.easier: Use a shorter step, smaller range, or fingertip support.
exercises.harder: Increase the step height or add a slow three-second lowering phase.

exercises.name: Band lateral walk
exercises.dose: 2 to 3 sets of 8 to 12 steps each direction
exercises.how: Place a loop band above the knees or at the ankles. Keep a small bend in the hips and knees, then step sideways without letting the feet snap together.
exercises.easier: Move the band above the knees or take smaller steps.
exercises.harder: Use a stronger band or place it closer to the ankles.

exercises.name: Bridge
exercises.how: Lie on your back with knees bent. Press through the heels and lift the hips while keeping the pelvis level, then lower with control.
exercises.easier: Use a smaller lift or fewer repetitions.
exercises.harder: Add a loop band or progress toward a staggered bridge.

responseIntro: Keep discomfort mild, approximately 3 out of 10 or less, without limping or changing how you move. Symptoms should not be meaningfully worse the following morning. These numbers are practical monitoring guides, not validated universal thresholds.
green: Mild front-of-knee discomfort, normal movement quality, and no meaningful increase the next morning.
yellow: Pain rises above mild, mechanics change, or stairs and squatting are worse the next day. Reduce knee depth, step height, resistance, or total repetitions.
red: Stop and seek same-day urgent assessment for a kneecap dislocation, true locking, rapid swelling, inability to bear weight, or a new painful, hot, red, or swollen joint with or without fever.

progression.title: Stage 1: calm the workload
progression.text: Temporarily reduce provocative running, jumping, deep squatting, or hill volume while keeping general activity within tolerance.

progression.title: Stage 2: build repetitions
progression.text: Work toward the upper repetition range with controlled knee alignment before increasing depth, step height, band resistance, or weight.

progression.title: Stage 3: restore the activity
progression.text: Reintroduce running, jumping, stairs, or sport-specific loads in small steps while symptoms return to baseline by the next morning.

readyItems: Squats and stairs are becoming less sensitive.
The knee is not meaningfully worse the next morning.
Hip and knee exercises remain controlled at the top repetition range.
You can add one workload variable without a new limp or movement compensation.
evaluation: Schedule a visit if the diagnosis is uncertain, the kneecap repeatedly feels unstable, swelling or locking is present, or there is no meaningful improvement after six to eight weeks of a consistent program.

faqs.q: Should all knee bending be avoided?
faqs.a: No. The goal is to find a tolerable starting range and reload it progressively. Avoiding all knee bending can reduce capacity and delay return to the activities you value.

faqs.q: Should I strengthen the hip or the knee?
faqs.a: Knee-targeted exercise is well supported and should remain part of the plan. Hip exercise can be added based on symptoms, impairments, and tolerance. When loaded knee bending is poorly tolerated, a more hip-focused starting phase can be reasonable, followed by progressive knee-targeted loading.

faqs.q: Do I need a knee brace or taping?
faqs.a: Exercise and education are primary. Taping or a prefabricated foot orthosis can help selected patients in the short term when matched to the examination, but they do not replace progressive loading.

faqs.q: When can I run again?
faqs.a: Return gradually when walking, stairs, and starter strengthening are controlled and the next-morning response is stable. Increase only one running variable at a time.

title: Rotator Cuff-Related Shoulder Pain Home Exercise Program

video.title: Rotator Cuff Tear Rehab & Exercises (Shoulder Pain, Tendinitis, Impingement)
video.description: A visual overview of rotator cuff-related shoulder pain, symptom monitoring, and progressive shoulder exercise options.
video.caution: Despite the title, rotator cuff-related pain does not necessarily mean a tendon tear, and an imaging finding does not automatically explain symptoms or require surgery. This is not a postoperative repair protocol. Seek assessment after a sudden injury with marked weakness or inability to raise the arm.

metaDescription: Printable rotator cuff pain exercises for shoulder mobility and strength, with symptom rules, progression, and guidance on when to seek care.
kicker: Shoulder pain · Home exercise plan
h1: Rotator Cuff Pain Exercises for Shoulder Strength and Motion
summary: Controlled movement and resistance exercises are first-line care for rotator cuff-related shoulder pain. Start with two or three movements when the shoulder is especially painful, then progress range and resistance.

authorityItems.text: Comfortable motion before heavier loading
Progressive rotator cuff and shoulder blade strength
Night pain and next-morning response guide the dose

fitIntro: This starter program is intended for adults who have already been evaluated and told rotator cuff-related shoulder pain is the likely diagnosis. It is not a self-diagnosis tool, a postoperative protocol, or a substitute for individualized care.
fit: Nontraumatic pain with lifting, reaching, or lying on the shoulder, including many presentations labeled rotator cuff tendinopathy, calcific tendinopathy, or partial-thickness tearing.
assessFirst: A fall or sudden pull followed by major weakness, suspected full-thickness tear, dislocation, fracture, recent surgery, or symptoms mainly driven by the neck or nerves.
redFlags: Call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or another medical emergency. Seek same-day urgent assessment after trauma with immediate weakness, inability to raise the arm, deformity, rapidly progressive weakness, new or worsening numbness, feeling seriously unwell, or a new painful, hot, red, or swollen shoulder with or without fever or chills.
programHeading: Start with a manageable range, then add resistance.
programIntro: If the shoulder is especially painful, begin with the wall slide plus one resistance exercise. Add the remaining movements as the shoulder tolerates the program without a next-day flare.
frequency: Motion daily; strength 3 days per week
equipment: Wall, light resistance band, optional light dumbbell
checkpoint: Reassess after 6 weeks; full trial 6 to 12 weeks
goal: More comfortable reaching, lifting, sleeping, and sports activity

exercises.name: Wall slide
exercises.how: Place the forearms on a wall. Gently slide upward while keeping the neck relaxed, without arching the lower back or lifting the ribs, then return slowly through a comfortable range.
exercises.easier: Use a smaller range or assist more with the other arm.
exercises.harder: Reach higher or add gentle pressure into a loop band.

exercises.name: Band external rotation
exercises.how: Keep the elbow at your side with a small towel between the arm and body. Rotate the forearm outward without twisting the trunk, then return slowly.
exercises.easier: Use a lighter band or a shorter range.
exercises.harder: Use a stronger band or slow the return for three seconds.

exercises.name: Band row
exercises.how: Anchor the band in front of you. Pull the elbows back while keeping the shoulders away from the ears, pause, then return with control.
exercises.easier: Stand closer to the anchor or use a lighter band.
exercises.harder: Increase band resistance or use a staggered stance.

exercises.name: Arm raise slightly forward from the side
exercises.how: Raise the arm about 30 degrees forward from the side with the thumb pointing up. Stop at a tolerated height, then lower slowly.
exercises.easier: Use no weight and a smaller range.
exercises.harder: Add a light dumbbell or gradually increase the height.

exercises.name: Wall push-up plus
exercises.how: Perform a wall push-up. At the top, gently push the wall away so the shoulder blades move around the ribs, without shrugging.
exercises.easier: Stand closer to the wall.
exercises.harder: Move from the wall to a sturdy counter, then gradually to a lower stable surface as strength improves.

responseIntro: Manageable discomfort is acceptable when it settles within a few hours and the shoulder is not worse the next morning.
green: Mild discomfort that settles within a few hours, with stable sleep and daily function the next morning.
yellow: Night pain, reaching, or daily function is worse the next day. Reduce range, resistance, repetitions, or the number of exercises.
red: Stop. Call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or another medical emergency. Seek same-day urgent assessment for sudden loss of strength, inability to raise the arm after trauma, deformity, new or worsening numbness, or a new painful, hot, red, or swollen shoulder with or without fever.

progression.title: Stage 1: restore comfortable motion
progression.text: Use assisted motion and low resistance. Avoid repeatedly testing the most painful range during the day.

progression.title: Stage 2: build cuff and shoulder blade strength
progression.text: Reach the top repetition range, then progress range first when appropriate, followed by band resistance or light external weight.

progression.title: Stage 3: restore overhead and task-specific load
progression.text: Progress incline pushing, carrying, reaching, throwing, or racquet work in small steps while the shoulder returns to its usual baseline by the next day.

readyItems: Daily reaching is easier and sleep is not worsening.
The exercise dose settles within a few hours.
You can control the full current range without shrugging or trunk compensation.
You can add range or resistance without a next-morning flare.
evaluation: Schedule a visit for traumatic weakness, progressive loss of function, persistent night pain, or substantial pain and disability that have not improved after an appropriate six- to twelve-week active rehabilitation trial.

faqs.q: Do I need an MRI before starting?
faqs.a: Usually not for a typical nontraumatic presentation. Imaging becomes more useful when trauma, major weakness, another diagnosis, or failure to improve would change management.

faqs.q: Should exercise be completely pain-free?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Manageable discomfort can be acceptable if it settles within a few hours and the shoulder is not worse the next morning.

faqs.q: Is a supervised program always better than home exercise?
faqs.a: Not always. The GRASP trial found that a supported home program performed similarly to a more intensive supervised progressive program over twelve months. Individual supervision remains valuable when the diagnosis, technique, progression, or adherence is difficult.

faqs.q: When should I consider an injection?
faqs.a: After an examination, a single subacromial corticosteroid injection may offer short-term pain relief when pain is blocking rehabilitation, but it does not replace exercise. Injectates are not interchangeable. Routine PRP use for rotator cuff tendinopathy or partial-thickness tears is not supported by the 2025 AAOS guideline, so the indication and uncertainty should be discussed individually.

title: Midportion Achilles Tendinopathy Home Exercise Program

video.title: Achilles Tendinopathy / Tendinitis / Tendinosis | Heel Pain Rehab (Education, Myths, Exercises)
video.description: A visual overview of Achilles tendinopathy, load monitoring, calf strengthening, and staged return to faster activity.
video.caution: The video discusses both midportion and insertional Achilles tendinopathy. This page is specifically for midportion pain. Keep early loading on a flat floor, and do not add step-deficit raises or hopping before slow strength and daily activity are stable.

metaDescription: Printable Achilles tendinopathy exercises for progressive calf loading, symptom monitoring, return to activity, and guidance on when to seek care.
kicker: Achilles tendon · Home exercise plan
h1: Midportion Achilles Tendinopathy Exercises
summary: Progressive tendon loading is first-line care for midportion Achilles tendinopathy. This plan uses straight-knee and bent-knee calf work, gradual resistance, and morning stiffness as a load signal.

authorityItems.text: Progressive calf strengthening at least three days per week
Next-morning pain and stiffness guide progression
Return to running and jumping after building a strength base

proof.span: straight knee, bent knee, and progression
or more of tendon loading each week

fitIntro: This starter program is intended for adults who have already been evaluated and told midportion Achilles tendinopathy is the likely diagnosis. It is not for postoperative recovery, a suspected rupture, or insertional pain without modification.
fit: Gradual-onset, load-related pain about 2 to 6 centimeters above the heel attachment, often with morning stiffness and sometimes with localized thickening.
assessFirst: Pain directly at the heel attachment, a sudden injury, substantial swelling, inability to perform a heel raise, recent surgery, uncertainty about rupture, or a known inflammatory, endocrine, or metabolic disorder. Stop tendon-loading exercise and contact the prescribing clinician immediately for new Achilles pain, swelling, or weakness during fluoroquinolone treatment. FDA-approved fluoroquinolone medication guides direct patients to stop the medicine at the first tendon symptoms and obtain prompt medical guidance. If symptoms begin after the course has ended, seek prompt assessment. Age over 60, systemic corticosteroid treatment, or a kidney, heart, or lung transplant increases concern.
redFlags: Call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or another medical emergency. Seek same-day urgent assessment for new one-sided calf warmth or swelling, or for a sudden pop, bruising, a palpable gap, inability to push off or perform a heel raise, acute major swelling, or other signs of tendon rupture.
programHeading: Use two calf angles and one clear progression.
programIntro: Perform the straight-knee and bent-knee loading exercises on the same day. Use the isometric hold as an entry option on more painful days, not as mandatory extra volume. When you reach the single-leg heel-raise progression, use it in place of the slow straight-knee heel raise rather than as extra volume. Keep all work on a flat floor for this midportion starter plan.
frequency: Loading at least 3 days per week
equipment: Wall or counter, chair, optional backpack or dumbbell
checkpoint: Commit to at least 12 weeks
goal: Stronger push-off, walking, stairs, running, and jumping

exercises.name: Optional calf-raise isometric hold
exercises.how: Rise onto both forefeet on a flat floor and hold at a comfortable height while using a counter for balance. Keep pressure even across the forefoot.
exercises.easier: Hold lower or shift more weight to the less painful side.
exercises.harder: Shift more weight toward the involved side.

exercises.name: Slow straight-knee heel raise
exercises.how: With knees straight and support nearby, rise for two to three seconds and lower for two to three seconds. Start with both legs.
exercises.easier: Use more hand support or a smaller range.
exercises.harder: Progress to one leg, then add a backpack or dumbbell.

exercises.name: Slow bent-knee heel raise
exercises.how: Keep a small, steady bend in both knees while lifting and lowering the heels slowly. Keep the knees over the middle toes.
exercises.easier: Use a wall sit position with a smaller heel lift.
exercises.harder: Shift toward one leg or add external load.

exercises.name: Single-leg heel raise progression
exercises.how: Use this in place of the slow straight-knee heel raise when ready. Rise and lower on one leg with a slow tempo, stable ankle, and similar heel height across repetitions.
exercises.easier: Use the other foot lightly for assistance.
exercises.harder: Add load while preserving height and control.

exercises.name: Later-stage pogo or hop
exercises.frequency: 2 to 3 days per week when ready
exercises.how: Begin with small two-leg springing contacts. Keep the rhythm quiet and controlled. Add this only after walking, stairs, and repeated single-leg heel raises are tolerated.
exercises.easier: Use brisk marching or quick heel raises without leaving the floor.
exercises.harder: Progress toward single-leg or activity-specific hopping.

responseIntro: Some tendon discomfort during loading can be acceptable when mechanics remain controlled and next-morning pain or stiffness does not increase. Complete rest is usually unnecessary.
green: Tolerable discomfort, good heel-raise control, and morning pain or stiffness that is unchanged or improving.
yellow: Next-morning pain or stiffness increases, the heel-raise height falls, or running and strengthening together create a cumulative flare. Reduce load or total contacts.
red: Stop. Call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or another medical emergency. Seek same-day urgent assessment for new one-sided calf swelling, a sudden pop, new bruising, a palpable gap, or inability to push off.

progression.title: Stage 1: establish a tolerable load
progression.text: Use two-leg slow raises and optional isometric holds. Continue general activity within pain tolerance rather than resting completely.

progression.title: Stage 2: increase tendon strength
progression.text: Progress from two legs to one leg, then add external load. Choose a resistance that makes the final repetitions challenging while controlled.

progression.title: Stage 3: restore spring and sport
progression.text: Add fast calf work, pogo contacts, hopping, and running volume only after slow strength and daily activities are stable.

readyItems: You have completed the progressive loading stage needed for the activity you plan to resume.
Pain stays at 5 out of 10 or less during activity and returns to baseline by the next morning.
Pain and stiffness are not increasing from week to week.
Walking, stairs, and repeated heel raises are controlled without a sustained flare.
These markers guide progression but do not independently clear high-demand or competitive sport.
evaluation: Schedule a visit if the pain is at the heel attachment, the diagnosis is uncertain, symptoms are worsening, a rupture is possible, or a consistent twelve-week loading trial does not improve function.

faqs.q: Should I stretch the tendon over the edge of a step?
faqs.a: Not automatically. This midportion starter plan uses a flat floor. Heel drops below a step can aggravate insertional Achilles pain and should be matched to the diagnosis.

faqs.q: Do I need eccentric heel drops specifically?
faqs.a: No. Eccentric, concentric, heavy slow resistance, and combined loading can all work. The important principle is progressive tendon loading at a challenging, tolerated intensity.

faqs.q: Must I stop running completely?
faqs.a: Usually not. Continue activity within pain tolerance when the next-morning response is stable. Reduce running volume or intensity if it repeatedly drives a flare.

faqs.q: How long does recovery take?
faqs.a: Commit to at least a twelve-week loading trial. Recovery commonly takes three to six months, and return to higher-demand sport may take longer.

title: Gluteal Tendinopathy Home Exercise Program
conditionName: Gluteal tendinopathy and lateral hip pain

video.title: Gluteal Tendinopathy / Greater Trochanteric Hip Bursitis (Education | Myths | Exercises)
video.description: A visual overview of lateral hip pain, compressive positions, load management, and progressive hip strengthening.
video.caution: The title includes bursitis, but this page is written for a diagnosed gluteal tendinopathy pattern rather than assuming isolated bursal inflammation. Treat the exercise examples as a menu, not extra volume. Delay step-ups, prolonged single-leg work, hills, running, or advanced options if night pain or next-day walking pain worsens.

metaDescription: Printable gluteal tendinopathy exercises for lateral hip pain, with load management, hip strengthening, symptom rules, and clear progression.
kicker: Lateral hip pain · Home exercise plan
h1: Gluteal Tendinopathy Exercises for Lateral Hip Pain
summary: Education plus progressive exercise is first-line care for gluteal tendinopathy. This plan pairs practical position changes with hip and lower-limb strengthening.

authorityItems.text: Reduce sustained compression at the side of the hip
Three days of progressive hip strengthening each week
Use night pain as a load-management signal

fitIntro: This starter program is intended for adults who have already been evaluated and told gluteal tendinopathy is the likely diagnosis. It is not a self-diagnosis tool, a postoperative protocol, or a substitute for individualized care.
fit: Pain and tenderness around the greater trochanter, often aggravated by side-lying, prolonged walking, stairs, or standing on one leg.
assessFirst: Groin-dominant pain, major hip stiffness, rapidly progressive weakness, a substantial limp, recent trauma, lumbar nerve symptoms, or a diagnosis that remains uncertain.
redFlags: Call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or another medical emergency. Seek same-day urgent assessment after acute trauma with inability to bear weight, rapidly progressive hip weakness, a new or rapidly worsening pronounced hip drop or limp, fever, deep groin pain with major motion loss, or new neurologic symptoms. Arrange a prompt evaluation for unexplained systemic or persistent night pain.
programHeading: Change the positions, then train the hip.
programIntro: Temporarily reduce compressive positions such as lying on the painful side, crossing the legs, hanging on one hip, and forceful stretching that pulls the painful leg across the body. Use the isometric on lighter days and the strength movements on nonconsecutive loading days.
frequency: Isometric most days; strength 3 nonconsecutive days per week
equipment: Stable chair, wall, optional loop band or belt
checkpoint: Initial trial of 8 weeks
goal: More comfortable sleep, walking, stairs, and single-leg tasks

exercises.name: Hip abduction isometric
exercises.how: Sit with a loop band or belt around the thighs. Press the knees gently outward without moving, hold, then relax. Keep the feet grounded.
exercises.easier: Use less pressure or a shorter hold.
exercises.harder: Increase the hold or band resistance without increasing night pain.

exercises.name: Bridge
exercises.how: Lie on your back with knees bent. Press through the heels, lift the hips while keeping the pelvis level, then lower slowly.
exercises.easier: Use a smaller range.
exercises.harder: Add a band, use a staggered stance, or progress toward an offset bridge.

exercises.name: Sit to stand or shallow squat
exercises.how: Keep the feet grounded and knees tracking over the middle toes as you stand from a chair or perform a shallow squat.
exercises.easier: Use a higher chair or push lightly from the armrests.
exercises.harder: Lower the chair or hold light external weight.

exercises.name: Band sidestep
exercises.dose: 2 sets of 8 to 12 steps each direction
exercises.how: Place a loop band above the knees or at the ankles. Take controlled side steps while keeping the pelvis level and feet facing forward.
exercises.easier: Move the band above the knees or take smaller steps.
exercises.harder: Use a stronger band or place it closer to the ankles.

exercises.name: Standing band hip abduction
exercises.dose: 2 sets of 8 to 12 repetitions per side
exercises.how: Hold a counter. Move one leg slightly out to the side without leaning the trunk or turning the toes outward, then return slowly.
exercises.easier: Use no band and a smaller range.
exercises.harder: Increase band resistance or pause at the end range.

responseIntro: Some discomfort can be acceptable when it does not increase night pain or next-day symptoms. Night pain is a useful signal that total walking, standing, and exercise load may be too high.
green: Mild, controlled discomfort with stable sleep and no meaningful increase in next-day lateral hip pain.
yellow: Night pain or next-day walking pain increases. Reduce resistance, range, repetitions, long walks, hills, or sustained single-leg positions.
red: Stop and seek same-day urgent assessment for new inability to bear weight, rapidly progressive weakness, deep groin pain with major stiffness, fever, or new neurologic symptoms.

progression.title: Stage 1: reduce compression
progression.text: Avoid lying directly on the painful side, crossing the legs, and hanging on one hip. Use a pillow between the knees when lying on the other side.

progression.title: Stage 2: build lower-limb strength
progression.text: Progress bridge, sit-to-stand, sidestep, and standing abduction by repetitions, band resistance, chair height, or external load.

progression.title: Stage 3: restore single-leg demand
progression.text: Add step-ups, longer walks, hills, and activity-specific single-leg tasks in small increments while night pain remains stable.

readyItems: Night pain is stable or improving.
Walking and stairs are becoming easier.
The pelvis stays level during the current exercises.
You can add resistance without a next-day lateral hip flare.
evaluation: Schedule a visit if groin pain or major stiffness suggests hip-joint disease, weakness or limping is progressing, neurologic symptoms are present, or an eight-week education and loading program is not improving function.

faqs.q: Should I stretch the outside of the hip?
faqs.a: Forceful hip-adduction stretching can compress the gluteal tendons and may aggravate symptoms. Early care usually emphasizes reducing compression and progressively strengthening instead.

faqs.q: How should I sleep?
faqs.a: Avoid lying directly on the painful side. When lying on the other side, place a pillow between the knees to reduce hip adduction and compression.

faqs.q: Is a corticosteroid injection the best first step?
faqs.a: Not usually. In the LEAP randomized trial, education plus exercise produced better global improvement than injection at eight weeks and maintained an advantage at longer follow-up.

faqs.q: Can I keep walking?
faqs.a: Usually yes, but adjust total distance, hills, and consecutive long days if night pain or next-day symptoms increase. Keep general activity while the strength program builds capacity.

sources.label: Mellor et al.: Education Plus Exercise Versus Corticosteroid Injection for Gluteal Tendinopathy, 2018
LEAP Trial Protocol: Exercise and Load-Management Program
LEAP-Ireland Feasibility Randomized Trial Results, 2026

title: Lateral Ankle Sprain Home Exercise Program

video.title: How to Rehab a Sprained Ankle (Start to Finish)
video.description: A visual overview of ankle-sprain rehabilitation from early motion and strength through balance, hopping, and return to sport.
video.caution: Use this only after fracture, high-ankle sprain, and Achilles concerns have been excluded. Do not force inversion early or progress to hopping, eyes-closed balance, or unstable surfaces before walking, stairs, swelling, and basic control have normalized.

metaDescription: Printable ankle sprain exercises for motion, strength, balance, brace use, symptom monitoring, and return-to-activity progression.
kicker: Ankle sprain · Home exercise plan
h1: Lateral Ankle Sprain Exercises
summary: Early protected weight bearing, range of motion, strength, and balance training support recovery after an uncomplicated lateral ankle sprain. This plan progresses from basic motion to controlled hopping.

authorityItems.text: Brace or tape when appropriate during early loading
Daily balance work to rebuild control
Function-based progression back to sport

proof.span: with strength three days per week
progress by ability, not only the calendar

fitIntro: This starter program is intended for adults who have already been evaluated and told an uncomplicated lateral ankle sprain is the likely diagnosis. Fracture, syndesmotic injury, Achilles rupture, and major midfoot injury should be reasonably excluded.
fit: Pain and swelling mainly at the outer ankle after a rolling injury, with improving ability to bear weight and no concerning fracture or signs of a high ankle sprain.
assessFirst: Inability to take four steps; tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either ankle bone, base of the fifth metatarsal, or navicular; pain or tenderness extending up the lower leg or at the proximal fibula; marked midfoot pain or swelling; bruising on the sole of the foot; recurrent instability; a suspected Achilles injury; or a severe injury that may need short immobilization.
redFlags: A newly cold, pale, blue, or numb foot after injury requires immediate emergency evaluation. Seek same-day urgent assessment for deformity, signs of Achilles rupture, inability to take four steps, tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either ankle bone, tenderness at the base of the fifth metatarsal or navicular, pain or tenderness at the proximal fibula, marked midfoot pain or swelling, bruising on the sole of the foot, or pain above the ankle. Arrange a prompt assessment for worsening swelling or bruising, locking, or repeated giving way.
programHeading: Move early, then rebuild ankle control and confidence.
programIntro: Progressive weight bearing with an appropriate brace or tape is supported for many uncomplicated sprains. Severe sprains may need clinician-directed immobilization for a short period before this progression.
frequency: Motion and balance daily; strength 3 days per week
equipment: Chair or counter, resistance band, optional brace
checkpoint: Reassess by function over 2 to 6 weeks
goal: Normal walking, stairs, balance, running, and cutting

exercises.name: Ankle pumps or alphabet
exercises.how: Move the ankle gently up, down, in, and out, or trace the alphabet with the toes. Stay within a comfortable range without forcing the injured direction.
exercises.easier: Use smaller motions with the leg supported.
exercises.harder: Increase the range as swelling and pain settle.

exercises.name: Band-resisted eversion
exercises.how: Anchor a band to the inside. Move the forefoot outward against the band without rotating the entire leg, then return slowly.
exercises.easier: Use a lighter band or shorter range.
exercises.harder: Use a stronger band or slower return.

exercises.name: Heel raise
exercises.how: Rise onto both forefeet with support nearby, keep the ankle centered, then lower slowly.
exercises.easier: Use more hand support or a smaller range.
exercises.harder: Progress to one leg or add external load.

exercises.name: Single-leg balance
exercises.how: Stand on the injured leg near a counter. Keep the heel and the bases of the big and little toes in contact with the floor while maintaining a steady posture with a soft knee.
exercises.easier: Use fingertip support or a shorter interval.
exercises.harder: Add head turns, reaches, or a less stable surface while keeping a stable support within reach. Do not use an unstable surface if you have meaningful fall risk.

exercises.name: Later-stage hop and hold
exercises.frequency: 2 to 3 days per week when ready
exercises.how: Make a small forward or side hop and land quietly on the injured leg. Hold the landing for two seconds before the next repetition.
exercises.easier: Use a step-and-hold without leaving the floor.
exercises.harder: Increase direction, distance, or sport-specific speed gradually.

responseIntro: Mild discomfort is acceptable, but not sharp pain, giving way, increased limping, or increased swelling later that day or the following morning.
green: Mild discomfort, improving walking, and swelling that is stable or decreasing by the next morning.
yellow: Limping, swelling, or pain is worse later that day or the next morning. Reduce walking volume, exercise range, resistance, or balance difficulty.
red: Stop. A newly cold, pale, blue, or numb foot after injury requires immediate emergency evaluation. Seek same-day urgent assessment for deformity, signs of Achilles rupture, inability to take four steps, sharp bony pain, pain or tenderness at the proximal fibula, marked midfoot pain or swelling, bruising on the sole of the foot, or pain above the ankle. Arrange a prompt assessment for repeated giving way.

progression.title: Stage 1: protect and restore motion
progression.text: Use an appropriate brace or tape, progressive weight bearing, and frequent comfortable motion. Avoid prolonged immobilization unless directed for a severe sprain.

progression.title: Stage 2: rebuild strength and balance
progression.text: Progress eversion, heel raises, and single-leg balance. Increase challenge only when walking and next-day swelling remain stable.

progression.title: Stage 3: restore speed and direction
progression.text: Add hopping, landing, running, cutting, and sport-specific tasks after normal walking, stairs, and basic single-leg control return.

readyItems: Walking and stairs are nearly normal without a growing limp.
Swelling does not increase the next morning.
Single-leg balance is controlled near support.
Small hops land quietly without pain or giving way.
evaluation: Seek same-day urgent assessment if you cannot take four steps, have focal tenderness over the ankle or midfoot bones, have pain above the ankle, deformity, or signs of Achilles rupture. Schedule a visit if instability keeps recurring or walking and swelling are not improving as expected. A newly cold, pale, blue, or numb foot after injury requires immediate emergency evaluation rather than a routine appointment.

faqs.q: Should I rest until all pain is gone?
faqs.a: Usually not. Early protected weight bearing and structured exercise are recommended for many uncomplicated sprains. The amount of protection depends on severity.

faqs.q: Do I need a brace?
faqs.a: A brace or tape can support early weight bearing and reduce recurrence risk, especially during higher-risk activity. The choice should match injury severity, comfort, and sport demands.

faqs.q: Is ice required?
faqs.a: Ice can be used briefly for comfort, but it should be an adjunct to exercise and progressive loading rather than the main treatment.

faqs.q: When can I return to sport?
faqs.a: Use function rather than the calendar alone. The decision should include pain during sport and over the prior 24 hours, ankle motion, strength, endurance and power, dynamic balance, confidence and perceived stability, psychological readiness, hopping and agility, sport-specific tasks, and tolerance of a full training session. No single cutoff guarantees readiness.

sources.label: JOSPT Clinical Practice Guideline: Lateral Ankle Ligament Sprains, 2021
BMJ: Home-Based Proprioceptive Training to Prevent Ankle-Sprain Recurrence
PAASS Return-to-Sport Consensus for Acute Lateral Ankle Sprain, 2021

title: Common Extensor Tendinopathy Home Exercise Program
shortTitle: Tennis elbow and common extensor exercises
conditionName: Lateral elbow tendinopathy and common extensor tendinopathy

video.title: Tennis Elbow Rehab (Education | Myths | Stretching & Strengthening Exercises)
video.description: A visual overview of lateral elbow tendinopathy, activity modification, and progressive wrist and grip loading.
video.caution: Static holds and slow wrist-extension loading are options within a progression, not two full daily programs to stack together. The video also discusses injections and surgery. Those decisions require individualized evaluation and are not part of this home program. Radiating pain, neck symptoms, or neurologic symptoms need an evaluation.

metaDescription: Printable tennis elbow exercises for common extensor tendinopathy, with progressive wrist loading, grip work, symptom rules, and return guidance.
kicker: Lateral elbow pain · Home exercise plan
h1: Tennis Elbow Exercises for Common Extensor Tendinopathy
summary: Activity adjustment and progressive wrist-extensor loading are commonly used first-line strategies. Average exercise benefits are modest and evidence certainty is low, so recovery and response vary.
authorityTitle: Settle symptoms. Build strength. Restore grip.

authorityItems.text: Progressive wrist-extensor loading
Grip and forearm capacity for daily tasks
A staged return to work, lifting, or sport

fitIntro: This starter program is intended for adults who have already been evaluated and told common extensor or lateral elbow tendinopathy is the likely diagnosis. It is not a self-diagnosis tool, a postoperative protocol, or a substitute for individualized care.
fit: Gradual pain and tenderness at or just below the outside elbow, aggravated by gripping, carrying, palm-down lifting, resisted wrist or finger extension, or stretching the wrist extensors.
assessFirst: A sudden injury, major swelling or weakness, inability to fully move the elbow, locking or instability, neck pain with radiating symptoms, numbness or tingling, or pain located farther down the forearm that may reflect radial nerve involvement.
redFlags: Call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or another medical emergency. Seek same-day urgent assessment for a sudden pop with bruising or deformity, rapidly increasing pain, marked or progressive weakness, or a new painful, hot, red, or swollen elbow with or without fever. Arrange a prompt evaluation for new numbness, persistent rest or night pain, or unexplained systemic symptoms.
programHeading: Load the wrist extensors, then restore the task.
programIntro: Guidelines support several ways to load the wrist extensors: holding without movement, lifting, and controlled lowering. No single dose is proven best. Use the static hold as the main load when the elbow is especially painful. As slow wrist extension becomes tolerable, use the hold as a warm-up rather than treating both exercises as full sessions on the same day.
frequency: Isometric daily when symptoms are sensitive; strength about 3 days per week
equipment: Table, light dumbbell or water bottle, towel or putty, optional band
checkpoint: Look for improvement by 4 to 6 weeks
goal: Comfortable grip, carrying, lifting, work, and sport

exercises.name: Isometric wrist extension
exercises.dose: 5 holds of 30 seconds with about 60 seconds of rest
exercises.frequency: Daily during the more painful phase
exercises.how: Support the forearm palm down with the wrist near neutral. Press the back of the hand into the opposite hand or a fixed surface without allowing movement. Use approximately 30 to 50 percent effort.
exercises.easier: Use 3 holds of 20 seconds at lighter effort.
exercises.harder: Build to 5 holds of 45 seconds, then increase resistance gradually.

exercises.name: Slow wrist extension
exercises.frequency: Every other day, usually 3 days per week
exercises.how: Support the forearm palm down with the hand over a table edge. Raise the wrist for 2 seconds and lower for 3 to 4 seconds. Keep the fingers relaxed.
exercises.easier: Use 2 sets of 10 with less weight or assist the lifting phase with the other hand.
exercises.harder: After two stable sessions, add the smallest available weight while keeping the slow tempo.

exercises.name: Forearm pronation and supination
exercises.dose: 2 sets of 12 repetitions in each direction
exercises.how: Keep the elbow at 90 degrees against the side. Slowly rotate a light hammer or dumbbell from palm up to palm down without moving the upper arm.
exercises.easier: Use no weight or hold closer to the weighted end.
exercises.harder: Hold farther from the weighted end, then add load.

exercises.name: Controlled grip
exercises.dose: 3 sets of 8 squeezes with a 5-second hold
exercises.how: Squeeze a rolled towel or soft putty at submaximal effort. Keep the wrist straight rather than bending it back during the squeeze.
exercises.easier: Use a lighter squeeze or a 3-second hold.
exercises.harder: Use firmer putty, then progress to short loaded carries with a neutral wrist.

exercises.name: Band row with a neutral wrist
exercises.how: Use a relaxed grip, keep the wrist straight, and draw the shoulder blade gently back without shrugging or clenching the band.
exercises.easier: Use a lighter band or 2 sets of 10.
exercises.harder: Use a stronger band or progress to a controlled single-arm row.

responseIntro: A small amount of familiar discomfort can be acceptable when it stays controlled, does not increase across repetitions, and returns to baseline by the next morning. These numbers are practical monitoring guides, not validated universal thresholds.
green: Pain stays between 0 and 3 out of 10, grip remains steady, and symptoms return to baseline by the following morning.
yellow: Pain reaches 4 to 5 out of 10, grip feels weaker afterward, or the elbow remains worse the next morning. Return to the prior tolerated dose or reduce one or more loading variables and add recovery time.
red: Stop and seek prompt assessment for sharp, electric, or rapidly increasing pain, new numbness or weakness, major swelling, loss of motion, or symptoms that worsen week to week. Use same-day urgent care for rapidly progressive weakness or a new painful, hot, red, or swollen elbow with or without fever.

progression.title: Stage 1: settle symptoms
progression.text: Reduce repetitive hard gripping and palm-down lifting. Use a neutral grip or palm-up lifting when practical and begin comfortable isometrics.

progression.title: Stage 2: build forearm capacity
progression.text: Add slow wrist extension, rotation, and controlled grip every other day. Progress repetitions before adding weight.

progression.title: Stage 3: return to work and sport demands
progression.text: Progress lever length, loaded carries, work tools, racquet handling, or lifting. Begin near half of your usual volume and increase only when symptoms return to baseline by the next day.

readyItems: Elbow and wrist motion are full or nearly full.
Daily tasks stay at 0 to 2 out of 10 without a next-day flare.
Resisted wrist extension and gripping stay controlled.
Two to three loading sessions and two graded task sessions do not escalate symptoms.
evaluation: Schedule a visit if neurologic or mechanical symptoms are present, pain is worsening, grip strength is progressively declining, or a correctly dosed program does not produce meaningful improvement after about four to six weeks.

faqs.q: Do I need complete rest?
faqs.a: Usually not. Reduce the most provocative gripping and lifting dose while keeping tolerable movement and progressive loading.

faqs.q: Should I stretch the forearm?
faqs.a: Gentle stretching is optional and should not provoke a sustained flare. Stretching alone has not shown durable superiority over a loading-based plan.

faqs.q: Will a counterforce strap help?
faqs.a: A strap or wrist support may improve pain during an activity for some people, but long-term benefit is uncertain and it should not replace progressive loading.

faqs.q: Do I need imaging?
faqs.a: Imaging is not routinely required for a typical presentation. It becomes more useful after trauma, with mechanical or neurologic findings, or when appropriate care has not worked.

title: Common Flexor Tendinopathy Home Exercise Program
shortTitle: Golfer's elbow and common flexor exercises
conditionName: Medial elbow tendinopathy and common flexor tendinopathy

video.title: Golfer’s Elbow Rehab (Education | Myths | Stretching & Strengthening Exercises)
video.description: A visual overview of medial elbow tendinopathy, activity modification, and progressive wrist, grip, and upper-limb loading.
video.caution: Do not stack the video’s full exercise menu onto this page’s dose. Acute throwing pain, lost velocity or instability, snapping, or ring- and small-finger symptoms need ligament or nerve assessment. Throwers also need a separate interval throwing plan.

metaDescription: Printable golfer's elbow exercises for common flexor tendinopathy, with wrist-flexor and pronator loading, grip work, and symptom guidance.
kicker: Medial elbow pain · Home exercise plan
h1: Golfer's Elbow Exercises for Common Flexor Tendinopathy
summary: Common flexor tendinopathy can improve with activity adjustment and progressive loading of the wrist flexors and pronators. Because medial-elbow exercise research is limited, this plan uses a conservative dose and clear reasons to seek assessment.

authorityItems.text: Progressive wrist-flexor and pronator loading
Stop signs for nerve symptoms and throwing instability
A gradual return to grip and task demand

fitIntro: This starter program is intended for adults who have already been evaluated and told common flexor or medial elbow tendinopathy is the likely diagnosis. It is not appropriate for a suspected ulnar collateral ligament injury or ulnar neuropathy.
fit: Gradual focal pain and tenderness at or just below the inside elbow, aggravated by gripping, resisted wrist flexion, forearm pronation, or stretching into wrist extension.
assessFirst: A sudden throwing injury, loss of throwing velocity, a feeling that the inner elbow is unstable during throwing, numbness or tingling into the ring and small fingers, hand weakness, snapping at the medial elbow, major swelling, locking, or neck symptoms radiating into the arm.
redFlags: Call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or another medical emergency. Seek same-day urgent assessment for a sudden pop with bruising or deformity, marked or progressive hand weakness, acute throwing-related instability, or a new painful, hot, red, or swollen elbow with or without fever. Arrange a prompt evaluation for persistent ring-finger or small-finger numbness, unexplained rest or night pain, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms.
programHeading: Strengthen the forearm while watching for signs of nerve or ligament injury.
programIntro: Direct exercise evidence for medial elbow tendinopathy is more limited than it is for lateral elbow pain. Slow wrist-flexor loading has the best condition-specific support, while the exact dose, grip work, rotation, and shoulder exercise are reasonable starting points.
frequency: Isometric daily when symptoms are sensitive; strength about 3 days per week
equipment: Table, light dumbbell or hammer, towel or putty, optional band
checkpoint: Look for improvement by 4 to 6 weeks
goal: Comfortable grip, pulling, lifting, work, racquet, or golf demand

exercises.name: Isometric wrist flexion
exercises.dose: 5 holds of 30 seconds with about 60 seconds of rest
exercises.frequency: Daily during the more painful phase
exercises.how: Support the forearm palm up with the wrist near neutral. Press the palm into the opposite hand without allowing movement. Use approximately 30 to 50 percent effort.
exercises.easier: Use 3 holds of 20 seconds at lighter effort.
exercises.harder: Build to 5 holds of 45 seconds, then increase resistance gradually.

exercises.name: Slow wrist flexion
exercises.frequency: Every other day, usually 3 days per week
exercises.how: Support the forearm palm up with the hand over a table edge. Curl upward for 2 seconds and lower for 3 to 4 seconds.
exercises.easier: Use 2 sets of 10 with less weight or assist the upward phase with the other hand.
exercises.harder: After two stable sessions, add the smallest available weight while preserving the slow tempo.

exercises.name: Slow palm-down forearm rotation
exercises.how: Keep the elbow at 90 degrees. Start palm up and slowly turn palm down against a light hammer or band, then return with control.
exercises.easier: Use no weight or hold closer to the weighted end.
exercises.harder: Increase the lever length, then add load.

exercises.name: Controlled grip
exercises.dose: 3 sets of 8 squeezes with a 5-second hold
exercises.how: Squeeze a rolled towel or soft putty at submaximal effort. Keep the wrist straight and avoid maximal gripping.
exercises.easier: Use a lighter squeeze or a 3-second hold.
exercises.harder: Use firmer putty, then progress to short neutral-wrist carries.

exercises.name: Band row with a neutral wrist
exercises.how: Use a relaxed grip, keep the wrist straight, and draw the shoulder blade back without shrugging.
exercises.easier: Use a lighter band or 2 sets of 10.
exercises.harder: Use a stronger band or progress to a controlled single-arm row.

responseIntro: A small amount of familiar tendon discomfort can be acceptable when it stays controlled and returns to baseline by the next morning. Neurologic symptoms or throwing-related instability are not acceptable loading symptoms. These numbers are practical monitoring guides, not validated universal thresholds.
green: Pain stays between 0 and 3 out of 10, grip remains steady, and the elbow returns to baseline by the following morning.
yellow: Pain reaches 4 to 5 out of 10 or remains worse the next morning. Return to the prior tolerated dose or reduce one or more loading variables and allow more recovery.
red: Stop and seek prompt assessment for ring-finger or small-finger numbness, hand weakness, snapping, sharp pain, major swelling, or pain or a feeling of instability during throwing. Use same-day urgent care for progressive weakness or a new painful, hot, red, or swollen elbow with or without fever.

progression.title: Stage 1: settle symptoms
progression.text: Reduce hard gripping, repeated wrist flexion and palm-down rotation, and painful throwing. Begin comfortable isometric loading.

progression.title: Stage 2: build forearm capacity
progression.text: Add slow wrist flexion, palm-down rotation, and controlled grip every other day. Progress repetitions before adding load.

progression.title: Stage 3: restore the task
progression.text: Progress neutral-wrist carries, pulling, work tools, racquet or golf demand. Throwing athletes need ligament and nerve assessment plus a separate interval throwing plan.

readyItems: Elbow, forearm, and wrist motion are full and comfortable.
Daily activity stays at 0 to 2 out of 10 without a next-day flare.
Resisted wrist flexion, pronation, and gripping remain controlled.
Two to three loading sessions and two graded task sessions do not escalate symptoms.
evaluation: Schedule a visit for any nerve symptoms, snapping, pain on the inside of the elbow during throwing, instability, progressive weakness, or no meaningful improvement after about four to six weeks. Overhead athletes should be assessed before beginning an interval throwing program.

faqs.q: Is this only golfer's elbow?
faqs.a: No. Common flexor tendinopathy also occurs with work, lifting, climbing, racquet sports, and other repeated gripping or forearm tasks.

faqs.q: Can I keep using the arm?
faqs.a: Usually yes, with the most painful gripping, palm-down rotation, or throwing dose reduced. Mild, stable discomfort can be acceptable when symptoms return to baseline by the next morning.

faqs.q: Will a brace fix it?
faqs.a: A brace can be tried for short-term activity tolerance, but it should not replace progressive loading and task modification.

faqs.q: Why do throwers need an assessment first?
faqs.a: Pain on the inside elbow during throwing may reflect the ulnar collateral ligament, ulnar nerve, or other structures rather than an isolated tendon problem.

metaDescription: Printable frozen shoulder exercises for adhesive capsulitis, with mobility matched to pain and stiffness, symptom rules, and safe progression.
kicker: Frozen shoulder · Mobility matched to pain and stiffness
h1: Frozen Shoulder Exercises for Adhesive Capsulitis
summary: Frozen shoulder needs a different dose at different stages. Begin with brief, comfortable motion while pain and night symptoms dominate, then increase stretching time, active range, and strength as symptoms settle.
authorityTitle: Calm pain. Restore motion. Rebuild function.

authorityItems.text: Use night pain to choose the right exercise dose
Progress from assisted motion to longer end-range time
Add active motion and strength as pain settles

proof.span: of short mobility work each day
to reassess pain, sleep, and motion

fitIntro: This starter program is intended for adults who have already been evaluated and told adhesive capsulitis or frozen shoulder is the likely diagnosis. It is not a postoperative protocol and should not be used to explain every painful or stiff shoulder.
fit: Gradual, often atraumatic shoulder pain followed by loss of motion both when you move the shoulder yourself and when someone else moves it. Turning the arm outward is often especially limited, with night pain and difficulty dressing, grooming, or reaching.
assessFirst: Sudden weakness after trauma, passive motion that is relatively preserved, prior shoulder surgery, substantial shoulder arthritis, cervical or neurologic symptoms, recurrent instability, or a pattern that does not include progressive loss of passive motion.
redFlags: Call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or another medical emergency. Seek same-day urgent assessment after trauma with deformity or inability to raise the arm, rapidly progressive weakness, new or worsening numbness, or a new painful, hot, red, or swollen shoulder with or without fever. Arrange a prompt evaluation for unexplained weight loss or known cancer with new persistent pain.
programHeading: Match the exercises to how painful and sensitive the shoulder is.
programIntro: Use only the first two exercises when rest pain and night pain are high. Aggressive stretching beyond the pain threshold can be counterproductive during a more painful phase. Add longer holds, active motion, and strength as pain settles and stiffness becomes the dominant limitation.
frequency: Short mobility sessions 1 to 2 times daily; strength 2 to 3 days per week when tolerated
equipment: Table, wall, cane or broom handle, optional light band
checkpoint: Reassess pain, sleep, function, and motion after 4 to 6 weeks
goal: Easier sleep, dressing, grooming, reaching, and lifting

exercises.name: Supported table slide
exercises.how: Sit facing a table with the hand supported on a towel. Slide the hand forward as the trunk inclines, then return before the muscles tense or pain increases.
exercises.easier: Use a shorter range and pause only 1 to 5 seconds in a comfortable position.
exercises.harder: Gradually hold 10 to 30 seconds near a tolerable end range before adding force.

exercises.name: Cane-assisted external rotation
exercises.how: Lie on the back or sit supported with both elbows near the sides. Use the unaffected arm and cane to rotate the involved forearm outward without letting the elbow drift away.
exercises.easier: Use a smaller range with the arm fully supported and only a brief pause.
exercises.harder: Increase the hold toward 10 to 30 seconds, then increase range without forcing the arm.

exercises.name: Supine assisted elevation
exercises.how: Lie on the back, clasp the hands or hold a cane, and let the unaffected arm assist the involved arm overhead through a comfortable range.
exercises.easier: Stop well before pain or support the arm on a pillow.
exercises.harder: Increase elevation gradually, then use less help from the other arm.

exercises.name: Active wall slide
exercises.frequency: Daily when rest pain is settling
exercises.how: Place the hand or forearm on a wall and slide upward while keeping the neck relaxed. Lower slowly without shrugging or twisting the trunk.
exercises.easier: Use the other hand to assist or shorten the range.
exercises.harder: Reach higher or add a brief comfortable end-range pause.

exercises.name: Light band row
exercises.how: Use a comfortable range and light resistance. Draw the shoulder blades gently back while keeping the neck relaxed and avoiding trunk compensation.
exercises.easier: Use a 5 to 10 second isometric hold or a lighter band.
exercises.harder: Add repetitions, then resistance, only when the shoulder returns to its usual baseline by the next day.

responseIntro: Gentle pulling or mild discomfort can be acceptable when it settles promptly and does not meaningfully increase rest pain, night pain, or next-morning stiffness.
green: The mobility dose settles promptly, sleep is not worse, and the shoulder is no stiffer the next morning.
yellow: Pain stays elevated later that day, sleep worsens, or motion is worse the next morning. Reduce range, hold time, repetitions, or session frequency.
red: Stop. Call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or another medical emergency. Seek same-day urgent assessment for sudden weakness, new numbness, traumatic loss of function, or a new painful, hot, red, or swollen shoulder with or without fever.

progression.title: Stage 1: when rest and night pain are high
progression.text: Use brief, comfortable table slides and assisted outward rotation. Avoid prolonged or forceful stretching.

progression.title: Stage 2: as pain becomes less constant
progression.text: Increase hold duration gradually and add assisted elevation and active wall slides.

progression.title: Stage 3: when stiffness is the main limitation
progression.text: Build total time near the end of your comfortable range, active motion, light resistance, and task-specific reaching while the shoulder returns to its usual baseline by the next day.

progression.title: Stage 4: restore function
progression.text: Progress lifting, overhead work, dressing, grooming, and sport demands rather than measuring success by motion alone.

readyItems: Night pain is stable or improving.
The current mobility dose settles without a prolonged flare.
Range or daily function is improving.
One variable can increase without worse next-day stiffness.
evaluation: Schedule a review if the diagnosis is uncertain, symptoms escalate, or pain, sleep, function, and motion have not improved after four to six weeks. When early pain prevents meaningful exercise, discuss whether a shoulder-joint corticosteroid injection is appropriate for your health history. If you have diabetes, also discuss how to monitor blood glucose because a temporary rise can occur after the injection.

faqs.q: Should I force the shoulder to regain motion?
faqs.a: No. Stretch intensity should match how painful and sensitive the shoulder is. Brief pain-limited motion is safer early, while longer stretching near the end of your comfortable range is more appropriate once pain settles.

faqs.q: How long does frozen shoulder last?
faqs.a: Recovery commonly takes many months. Some people retain mild pain or motion loss at twelve to eighteen months even when disability is much better.

faqs.q: Do I need an MRI?
faqs.a: Usually not for a typical clinical pattern. Imaging is an adjunct when the presentation is atypical, trauma occurred, or another condition must be excluded.

faqs.q: Can an injection help?
faqs.a: A shoulder-joint corticosteroid injection can improve short-term pain and function, particularly earlier in the course, but it does not replace a staged mobility plan. If you have diabetes, ask how to monitor blood glucose afterward because a temporary rise can occur.
