video.title: Peroneal Tendinopathy / Tendinitis: Causes & Treatment (Education | Strengthening | Stretching)
video.description: The embedded chapter explains load modification and progressive ankle, calf, balance, and whole-leg strengthening for nontraumatic peroneal tendon pain.
video.caution: This video addresses nontraumatic peroneal tendinopathy. It does not replace evaluation after an acute injury or when there is snapping, tendon displacement, repeated giving way, marked weakness, or focal bone pain.

metaDescription: Printable peroneal tendinopathy exercises for outer ankle pain, with eversion strength, heel raises, balance, symptom rules, and graded activity.
kicker: Outer ankle tendon pain · Starter home exercise plan
h1: Peroneal Tendinopathy Exercises
summary: This evidence-informed program is for clinician-evaluated, nontraumatic peroneal tendon pain along the outer ankle or foot. It builds eversion strength, calf capacity, balance, and tolerance for walking or sport.

authorityItems.text: Not for a fracture, acute tear, or snapping tendon
Five progressive foot, ankle, and leg movements
Level activity before hills, trails, and cutting

proof.span: eversion, calf, balance, and leg control
to look for an improving trend

fitIntro: Use this plan only when peroneal tendinopathy is the established or strongly suspected diagnosis. Lateral ankle pain can also come from bone, cartilage, ligaments, nerves, the subtalar joint, a tendon tear, or tendon instability.
fit: Gradual outer ankle or lateral foot pain linked to walking, running, hills, uneven ground, or a recent training increase, with tenderness along the tendons behind the outer ankle and symptoms reproduced by turning the foot outward against resistance.
assessFirst: A recent inversion injury or high-force event, inability to take four steps, focal bone tenderness at the outer ankle or base of the fifth metatarsal, marked bruising or swelling, a pop followed by weakness, snapping behind the outer ankle, recurrent giving way, a slow-to-recover ankle sprain, burning, numbness, foot drop, or unexplained rest or night pain.
redFlags: Call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or another medical emergency. Seek same-day urgent assessment for inability to bear weight after trauma, visible deformity, rapidly increasing swelling, a hot red swollen ankle or foot with or without fever, a wound with spreading redness, or severe unrelenting pain. Arrange prompt assessment for a new pop with weakness, repeated snapping or tendon displacement, recurrent giving way, new numbness or foot drop, focal bone pain, or progressive rest or night pain.
programHeading: Build outer ankle capacity without instability.
programIntro: Condition-specific exercise trials are sparse, so the exact dose is a practical starting point based on consensus, tendon-loading principles, and function. Use flat, predictable surfaces first. A snapping or displaced tendon, acute tear, fracture, or unstable ankle needs assessment rather than unsupervised loading.
frequency: Strength 2 to 3 nonconsecutive days per week; balance 3 to 5 days per week
equipment: Resistance band, stable chair or rail, low step, and optional weight
checkpoint: Review the trend at 6 weeks; continue loading for 8 to 12 weeks or longer
goal: Comfortable walking, hills, uneven ground, running, or sport

exercises.name: Banded ankle eversion
exercises.how: Sit with a band around the forefoot and anchored toward the opposite side. Keep the knee and thigh still, turn the sole gently outward through a comfortable range, then return over about three seconds.
exercises.easier: Use a lighter band or four holds of 20 to 30 seconds without movement.
exercises.harder: Use a heavier band, slow the return, or perform side-lying eversion with a light ankle weight.

exercises.name: Heel raise
exercises.how: Rise as high as you can control and lower slowly while keeping pressure through both the big-toe and little-toe sides of the forefoot rather than rolling outward.
exercises.easier: Use both legs and hand support.
exercises.harder: Progress to one leg, then add weight or use a step.

exercises.name: Supported single-leg balance
exercises.dose: 3 rounds of 30 to 60 seconds per side
exercises.how: Stand near a stable support with the whole forefoot grounded and the knee softly bent.
exercises.easier: Use fingertip support or keep the other toes on the floor.
exercises.harder: Add a three-way reach, small trunk rotations, or a controlled single-leg hip hinge.

exercises.name: Low step-up to controlled step-down
exercises.dose: 2 to 3 sets of 8 to 12 repetitions per side
exercises.how: Step onto a low stable step without pushing from the back leg, stand tall, then lower slowly with the foot and knee controlled.
exercises.easier: Use a lower step and a rail.
exercises.harder: Use a lateral or forward step-down, a slightly taller step, or light weight.

exercises.name: Level walking or cycling base
exercises.dose: Start with a repeatable 10 to 20 minutes
exercises.how: Choose flat walking or cycling that does not cause a sustained flare. Keep terrain and effort predictable while you establish a repeatable baseline.
exercises.easier: Split the time into two shorter sessions.
exercises.harder: Add two to five minutes first, then speed, hills, uneven ground, or trail exposure one variable at a time.

responseIntro: Mild discomfort can be acceptable when technique remains stable, there is no snapping or giving way, and symptoms return to their usual baseline by the next morning.
green: Mild discomfort, stable technique, no snapping or giving way, and symptoms return to their usual baseline by the next morning.
yellow: Pain, swelling, limping, or fatigue is meaningfully worse later that day or the next morning without snapping or giving way. Reduce range, resistance, repetitions, steps, or terrain by about 25 to 50 percent and rebuild.
red: Stop for sharp pain, a pop, tendon snapping or displacement, new weakness, giving way, numbness, marked swelling, or inability to bear weight. Obtain an assessment.

progression.title: Stage 1: settle and reload
progression.text: Reduce hills, cambered roads, trail running, and cutting. Use isometric or light eversion, double-leg heel raises, supported balance, and level activity.

progression.title: Stage 2: build capacity
progression.text: Progress to moving eversion, single-leg heel raises, step-downs, and dynamic balance. Add one variable only after several stable sessions.

progression.title: Stage 3: restore the goal
progression.text: Add weighted heel raises, heavier eversion, three-way reaches or hip hinges, brisk level walking, then graded walk-jog or terrain exposure.

progression.title: Stage 4: add energy storage when sport requires it
progression.text: Progress from double-leg to single-leg pogos, then forward and lateral line hops and controlled cutting. This stage is optional and should not begin when snapping or instability is present.

readyItems: Thirty minutes of brisk level walking and normal stairs do not worsen the next morning.
Twenty controlled single-leg heel raises can be completed without rolling outward or snapping.
Single-leg balance can be held for 45 to 60 seconds.
Ten controlled step-downs can be completed without giving way.
For impact goals, first 20 small double-leg pogos and then 20 small single-leg pogos on the involved side do not cause sharp pain or instability.
These are practical progression guides, not validated return-to-sport cutoffs.
evaluation: Schedule a reassessment for worsening symptoms, recurrent swelling, snapping, repeated sprains or giving way, inability to progress heel raises, inability to resume normal walking, or no improving trend after about six weeks.

faqs.q: Is this just an ankle sprain?
faqs.a: They can coexist. Persistent pain behind the outer ankle, weakness, or snapping after a sprain needs reassessment because tendon injury or instability may be present.

faqs.q: Should I rest completely?
faqs.a: Usually use relative load reduction rather than prolonged complete rest, unless a clinician suspects a fracture, rupture, or instability or recommends temporary immobilization.

faqs.q: Can I run?
faqs.a: Begin flat walk-jog intervals only after level walking and the strength guideposts are tolerated. Reintroduce speed, hills, cambered roads, and trails separately.

faqs.q: What shoes or orthotics help?
faqs.a: Choose a stable, comfortable shoe. Avoid an insert that forces the foot farther outward or increases instability. Posting or bracing should be individualized after alignment and ankle stability are assessed.

faqs.q: Do I need imaging?
faqs.a: Not routinely when the examination is clear and recovery is progressing. Ultrasound or MRI may be useful when snapping, a tear, instability, bony pathology, or an atypical course is suspected.

title: Tibialis Posterior Tendinopathy Home Exercise Program

video.title: Tibialis Posterior Tendinopathy | Tendinitis | Dysfunction | Pain (Exercises, Rehab, Strengthening)
video.description: The embedded chapter explains activity adjustment, supportive options, and progressive foot, calf, balance, and whole-leg exercise for tibialis posterior tendon pain.
video.caution: New arch collapse, inability to perform a heel raise, acute trauma, marked swelling, or suspected progressive collapsing foot deformity requires examination rather than unsupervised progression.

metaDescription: Printable posterior tibial tendon pain exercises, with arch support guidance, heel raises, balance, symptom rules, and warnings for progressive foot collapse.
kicker: Inner ankle and arch tendon pain · Starter home exercise plan
h1: Posterior Tibial Tendon Pain Exercises
summary: This progressive program is for clinician-evaluated pain of the tibialis posterior tendon along the inner ankle or arch, without a new rupture or progressive foot collapse. Supportive footwear or an orthosis may be an important companion to exercise.

authorityItems.text: New arch collapse or heel-raise weakness needs assessment
Five tendon, calf, balance, and leg movements
Footwear or an orthosis may be part of treatment

proof.span: tendon, calf, balance, and leg capacity

fitIntro: This is an early-stage starter plan, not a self-diagnosis tool and not stand-alone treatment for progressive collapsing foot deformity. A new change in arch shape or heel alignment, inability to perform a single-leg heel raise, or increasing weakness should be assessed before exercise is advanced.
fit: Load-related pain or tenderness behind the inner ankle bone and into the arch, often worse with prolonged walking, running, hills, stairs, or heel raises, with preserved or only mildly reduced push-off and no progressive deformity.
assessFirst: Recent trauma or a pop, inability to perform a single-leg heel raise, clear loss of heel-rise height or endurance, new or increasing arch flattening, the heel drifting outward, the forefoot turning outward, rigid deformity, lateral ankle impingement pain, marked swelling, inability to walk normally, focal navicular bone tenderness, pain with hopping after a training increase, burning, numbness, or a hot swollen foot in diabetes or neuropathy.
redFlags: Call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or another medical emergency. Seek same-day urgent assessment for inability to bear weight after trauma, visible or rapidly progressive deformity, a hot red markedly swollen foot with or without fever, especially with diabetes or reduced sensation, a wound with spreading redness, or severe unrelenting pain. Arrange prompt evaluation for a pop with sudden loss of push-off, new arch collapse, inability to perform a heel raise, rapidly increasing weakness, focal navicular bone pain, new numbness, or progressive rest or night pain.
programHeading: Load the tendon while watching the shape and function of the foot.
programIntro: The best exercise dose is uncertain. Small trials mainly studied strengthening together with foot orthoses and stretching, not exercise in isolation. A supportive shoe, arch support, brace, or temporary immobilization may be appropriate based on walking tolerance and deformity and should be individualized.
frequency: Strength 2 to 3 nonconsecutive days per week; balance 2 to 3 days per week
equipment: Resistance band, supportive shoe, stable support, optional small ball and weight
checkpoint: Review the trend at 6 weeks; build for 8 to 12 weeks or longer
goal: Restore push-off, walking, stairs, hills, and appropriate return to running

exercises.name: Banded foot adduction
exercises.how: Sit with both knees bent and the foot in a supportive shoe. Anchor a band outside the forefoot at about 45 degrees to the floor. Keep the heel and leg quiet, slide the forefoot inward, then return over three seconds without clawing the toes.
exercises.easier: Use no band, a shorter range, or four low-effort isometric holds of 20 seconds.
exercises.harder: Use a stronger band or a four-second return.

exercises.name: Heel raise with controlled heel direction
exercises.how: Keep the base of the big toe grounded, rise as high as controlled, allow the heels to turn slightly toward each other, then lower over three seconds. A small ball between the heels can guide the motion, but do not force an arch position.
exercises.easier: Use a seated or double-leg version with hand support.
exercises.harder: Progress to one leg, then add weight or use a step after 15 controlled repetitions.

exercises.name: Supported single-leg balance
exercises.dose: 3 rounds of 30 to 60 seconds per side
exercises.how: Stand near a stable support and let the foot move naturally within a tolerable range while the knee and pelvis remain controlled.
exercises.easier: Use fingertip support or keep the opposite toes on the floor.
exercises.harder: Add three-way reaches or slow trunk rotations.

exercises.name: Squat to chair or supported split squat
exercises.how: Keep the whole foot grounded and move through a comfortable range with a stable chair or rail nearby.
exercises.easier: Use a higher chair, shallower range, or more support.
exercises.harder: Use a lower chair, split squat or reverse lunge, then add light weight.

exercises.name: Supported single-leg hip hinge
exercises.dose: 2 to 3 sets of 6 to 12 repetitions per side
exercises.how: Stand on one leg near a stable support, soften the knee, hinge at the hip without twisting, then return upright with controlled foot pressure.
exercises.easier: Use kickstand toes and hand support.
exercises.harder: Progress to a single-leg deadlift, add a knee drive, or hold weight in the opposite hand.

responseIntro: Establish a repeatable daily step baseline. If walking is provocative, temporarily use cycling or swimming. Increase steps, pace, hills, or running one variable at a time while monitoring gait, push-off, swelling, and foot shape.
green: Mild discomfort, normal gait and push-off, no visible worsening of arch or heel position, and symptoms return to baseline by the next morning.
yellow: Medial ankle swelling, limping, walking tolerance, or next-morning pain is meaningfully worse. Reduce resistance, heel-raise range, repetitions, or daily steps by about 25 to 50 percent.
red: Stop for a pop, sudden weakness, inability to perform a heel raise, new or progressive arch collapse, focal bone pain, numbness, hot red swelling, or inability to bear weight. Obtain an assessment.

progression.title: Stage 1: reduce overload and establish support
progression.text: Track daily steps. Consider supportive footwear or clinician-directed arch support. Use banded adduction, seated or double-leg heel raises, and supported balance.

progression.title: Stage 2: build tendon and calf capacity
progression.text: Progress adduction resistance, double-leg to single-leg heel raises, and squat, split-squat, or hip-hinge strength. Advance only after several stable next mornings.

progression.title: Stage 3: restore walking and stairs
progression.text: Add weighted heel raises, dynamic balance, step and lunge demands, then brisk walking and hills one variable at a time.

progression.title: Stage 4: return to running or sport when appropriate
progression.text: Use a graded walk-jog progression, then optional pogos, hops, and cutting only when there is no progressive deformity or instability and the examination supports impact loading.

readyItems: Thirty minutes of level walking and normal stairs do not worsen the next morning.
Twenty controlled single-leg heel raises can be completed with useful height and the base of the big toe grounded.
The arch and heel position do not show progressive change during loading.
Single-leg balance can be held for 45 to 60 seconds.
Ten controlled step-downs can be completed without a sustained flare.
Impact begins only after 20 small pogos are tolerated and after clinician review when foot collapse was ever suspected.
evaluation: Schedule a reassessment for any new arch change, worsening push-off, recurrent swelling, inability to progress heel raises, no improving trend after six weeks, or persistent limits after eight to twelve weeks.

faqs.q: Do flat feet mean this tendon is diseased?
faqs.a: No. Flat or pronated feet can be pain free. A new painful change, progressive flattening, and loss of function matter more than appearance alone.

faqs.q: Will exercise rebuild a collapsed arch?
faqs.a: Exercise may improve pain and capacity, but it is not proven to reverse structural progressive collapsing foot deformity. New or progressive deformity needs assessment.

faqs.q: Do I need an orthotic?
faqs.a: Orthoses or braces can reduce tendon and arch demand, and most trials combined them with exercise. The device and duration should fit symptoms and deformity rather than foot appearance alone.

faqs.q: Can I run?
faqs.a: First restore level walking, heel-rise capacity, and next-day stability. Then use walk-jog intervals on flat ground and change one training variable at a time.

faqs.q: Should I stretch the calf?
faqs.a: Gentle calf mobility can be used when ankle motion is clearly limited and it does not increase inner ankle or arch pain. Do not force an aggressive stretch through the painful tendon.

title: Thumb CMC Osteoarthritis Home Exercise Program
seoTitle: Thumb CMC Osteoarthritis Exercises and Brace Guide
metaDescription: Printable thumb CMC osteoarthritis exercises and brace guidance, with joint protection, gentle strength, symptom rules, and clear progression.
kicker: Thumb-base arthritis · Home exercise and orthosis guide
h1: Thumb CMC Osteoarthritis Exercises
summary: Thumb carpometacarpal osteoarthritis affects the joint at the base of the thumb. A well-fitting thumb orthosis, practical changes to painful gripping and pinching, and progressive hand exercise can help function. Exercise benefits are usually modest, and no program can reverse the arthritis or rebuild cartilage.

authorityItems.text: Five low-load mobility and strength movements
A thumb-base orthosis is a core treatment option
Joint protection for gripping, pinching, and carrying

proof.span: mobility, thumb control, and useful pinch
of light strength work each week
to assess function and symptom change

fitIntro: This program is for adults who have been evaluated and told that thumb CMC osteoarthritis is the likely source of their symptoms. It is not a self-diagnosis tool or a postoperative protocol.
fit: Pain at the base of the thumb during opening jars, turning keys, writing, pinching, gripping, carrying, or prolonged phone use, sometimes with stiffness or reduced pinch strength.
assessFirst: An uncertain diagnosis, symptoms after a fall or collision, a thumb that catches, locks, dislocates, or repeatedly gives way, numbness, tingling, progressive weakness, pain mainly along the thumb side of the wrist rather than at the thumb base, several persistently swollen joints, prolonged morning stiffness, recent hand surgery, injection, or fracture, or severe unexplained rest or night pain.
redFlags: Call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or another medical emergency. Seek same-day care for a rapidly worsening hot, red, or markedly swollen joint, fever, a wound near the joint, new deformity after trauma, or inability to use the hand after injury. Remove a brace immediately if it causes numbness or color change. Seek urgent assessment if a finger or hand remains numb, cold, pale, blue, or weak after the brace is removed.
programHeading: Support the joint. Train the hand. Protect function.
programIntro: First-CMC orthoses are strongly recommended in the American College of Rheumatology guideline. Exercise evidence is more mixed and benefits are generally modest, so this plan combines comfortable movement and low-load strength with joint protection and an optional orthosis rather than presenting exercise as a cure.
frequency: Mobility most days; strengthening 2 to 3 days per week
equipment: Table, optional light elastic loop, soft sponge or putty, and a well-fitting thumb CMC orthosis if helpful
checkpoint: Review function and symptoms after 6 to 8 weeks
goal: Easier gripping, pinching, writing, opening, carrying, and daily hand use

exercises.name: Rounded thumb opposition
exercises.how: Support the forearm and keep the wrist straight. Bring the thumb pad toward the index fingertip to form a relaxed letter C. Keep the thumb joints softly bent and avoid squeezing. Hold for two to three seconds, then relax.
exercises.easier: Move only toward the index finger through a smaller range.
exercises.harder: Touch each fingertip in sequence. Reach toward the base of the small finger only when comfortable.

exercises.name: Gentle first web-space opening
exercises.how: Support the affected hand with the palm facing up. Use the other hand to gently guide the thumb away from the palm until a mild stretch is felt in the web space. Do not force the base joint or push into sharp pain.
exercises.easier: Use a smaller range and a 10-second hold.
exercises.harder: Progress toward a 30-second hold without increasing the force.

exercises.name: First dorsal interosseous index slide
exercises.how: Place the hand flat on a table with the palm down. Keep the other fingers relaxed. Slide the index finger sideways away from the middle finger, then return slowly without hard pinching.
exercises.easier: Use no resistance and a shorter slide.
exercises.harder: Add a very light elastic loop around the fingers.

exercises.name: Thumb palmar-abduction isometric
exercises.how: Hold the thumb in a relaxed C position in front of the palm. Place a finger from the opposite hand against the outside of the thumb. Gently press outward without allowing movement and keep the thumb knuckle from collapsing backward.
exercises.easier: Perform three five-second holds.
exercises.harder: Build to 10-second holds, then use a light elastic loop. Do not use maximal effort.

exercises.name: Controlled three-point pinch
exercises.frequency: 2 to 3 days per week, beginning in Stage 3
exercises.how: Use very soft therapy putty, a folded sponge, or a light clothespin. Pinch between the thumb pad and the pads of the index and middle fingers. Maintain a rounded C shape and avoid a forceful side or key pinch.
exercises.easier: Practice the position without resistance.
exercises.harder: Increase resistance slightly or practice the same alignment during a meaningful daily task.

responseIntro: Begin with one set when the thumb is irritable. Mild discomfort can be acceptable when movement remains controlled and symptoms return to their usual baseline by the next morning.
green: Mild discomfort up to about 3 out of 10, controlled movement, and symptoms return to their usual baseline by the next morning.
yellow: Pain is sharper, technique changes, aching or swelling is meaningfully worse later in the day, or symptoms remain worse the following morning. Reduce resistance, range, repetitions, or pinch practice.
red: Stop and seek assessment for rapidly increasing swelling, redness, heat, fever, new numbness, new deformity, sudden loss of strength, or severe pain after trauma.

progression.title: Stage 1: protect and move
progression.text: Use joint-protection strategies and a comfortable orthosis during aggravating tasks when helpful. Perform rounded opposition and gentle web-space opening.

progression.title: Stage 2: build control
progression.text: Add first dorsal interosseous work and light palmar-abduction isometrics. Reach the upper repetition range before adding resistance.

progression.title: Stage 3: restore useful pinch
progression.text: Add controlled three-point pinch and progressively practice buttons, utensils, writing, keys, food preparation, or another relevant task.

progression.title: Stage 4: maintain capacity
progression.text: Continue useful strength exercises twice weekly. Use the orthosis and adaptive equipment selectively rather than assuming they must be worn for every activity.

readyItems: Resting symptoms are stable.
Rounded opposition does not produce sharp pain.
The current dose has been tolerated for several sessions.
Symptoms return to baseline by the following morning.
The thumb maintains a rounded position without the knuckle collapsing backward.
Daily tasks are becoming easier or can be performed for longer.
evaluation: Schedule a hand or sports medicine evaluation if symptoms worsen, the orthosis causes pressure or numbness, function has not improved after six to eight weeks, deformity or instability is progressing, or the diagnosis remains uncertain.

faqs.q: Will these exercises reverse the arthritis?
faqs.a: No. Exercise does not regrow cartilage or remove arthritic changes. The goals are improved strength, movement control, function, and confidence.

faqs.q: What type of brace is best?
faqs.a: No single orthosis is clearly superior for every patient. A rigid CMC support may provide more stability, while neoprene may be more comfortable. Fit and usefulness during painful tasks matter more than a particular brand.

faqs.q: How should I use a thumb CMC brace?
faqs.a: A practical trial is to wear a comfortable, well-fitting orthosis during painful gripping or pinching and, if helpful, at night. Remove it immediately if it causes numbness, color change, skin injury, or increased pain. Seek urgent assessment if a finger or hand remains numb, cold, pale, blue, or weak after the brace is removed. Research has not established one universal wearing schedule.

faqs.q: Should I squeeze a ball?
faqs.a: Hard repetitive squeezing can aggravate the thumb base. Begin with the low-load exercises in this program and add soft, controlled pinch only after symptoms are stable.

faqs.q: How can I protect the joint during daily tasks?
faqs.a: Use larger handles and jar-opening aids, use the whole hand instead of forceful key pinch, carry with two hands, slide objects when possible, keep the wrist relatively neutral, and break prolonged gripping into shorter periods.

faqs.q: When would a hand therapist help?
faqs.a: A hand therapist can fit or fabricate an orthosis, distinguish thumb CMC pain from nearby tendon or nerve problems, and adapt the program for deformity, instability, work, music, sport, or high-demand hand use.

title: De Quervain Tenosynovitis Starter Program
seoTitle: De Quervain Exercises, Brace, and Activity Guide
shortTitle: De Quervain wrist and thumb program
metaDescription: De Quervain exercises, thumb-spica brace guidance, activity changes, symptom rules, and evidence-informed options for thumb-side wrist pain.
kicker: Thumb-side wrist pain · Assessment-first starter plan
h1: De Quervain Exercises and Activity Guide
summary: De Quervain tenosynovitis causes pain along the thumb side of the wrist, usually during thumb movement, gripping, lifting, or wrist deviation. Exercise evidence is limited, so this plan emphasizes diagnosis, activity modification, a short trial of a well-fitting thumb-spica orthosis, pain-free motion, and cautious loading.

authorityItems.text: Exercise alone has not been proven effective
Five cautious motion and loading options
Better-supported clinician treatments are explained

proof.span: to reassess an unclear or nonimproving course

fitIntro: This starter plan is for adults who have been evaluated and told De Quervain tenosynovitis is the likely diagnosis, or whose clinician has recommended a short trial of conservative care. Nearby joint, bone, nerve, and tendon conditions can produce similar symptoms.
fit: Localized tenderness and pain over the thumb side of the wrist during lifting, gripping, pinching, opening containers, using a phone, or caring for an infant.
assessFirst: An uncertain diagnosis, symptoms after a fall or direct blow, numbness, tingling, burning, progressive weakness, pain centered at the thumb-base joint, swelling or crepitus farther up the back of the forearm, a thumb that catches or locks, a visible mass, inflammatory arthritis, recent injection or surgery, or symptoms severe enough to prevent normal light hand use. Pregnancy and the postpartum period are not automatic exclusions, but brace fit, swelling, infant care, and loading should be individualized.
redFlags: Call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or another medical emergency. Seek same-day care for a hot, red, rapidly swelling area, fever, an open wound, new deformity, major loss of motion after trauma, or inability to use the hand. Arrange prompt assessment for new numbness, sudden weakness, or severe pain after injury.
programHeading: Settle the wrist. Maintain motion. Rebuild load carefully.
programIntro: Exercise has not been proven effective as a stand-alone treatment. Pain-free motion and thumb-extension isometrics appear feasible within multimodal care. Network meta-analyses, with important certainty limitations, favor a clinician-delivered corticosteroid injection combined with thumb-spica immobilization for about three to four weeks. Injection suitability and risks require an individual clinical discussion.
frequency: Pain-free motion 2 to 4 times per day; strengthening daily or every other day by stage
equipment: Table, optional very light elastic loop, light cup, and a comfortable thumb-spica orthosis if helpful
checkpoint: Seek reassessment if there is no clear improvement after 2 to 4 weeks
goal: Comfortable lifting, gripping, pinching, infant care, phone use, and daily hand tasks

exercises.name: Pain-free thumb bend and return
exercises.how: Support the forearm with the wrist straight. Slowly move the thumb toward the fingers through a comfortable range, then return it to the starting position. Do not force the thumb tightly into the palm.
exercises.easier: Use a smaller range.
exercises.harder: Touch the thumb to each fingertip while the wrist remains neutral.

exercises.name: Supported wrist flexion and extension
exercises.how: Rest the forearm on a table with the hand just beyond the edge. Slowly bend the wrist forward and backward through a comfortable range. Keep the movement straight rather than drifting toward either side.
exercises.easier: Rest the hand fully on the table and use a smaller range.
exercises.harder: Increase the comfortable range. Do not add weight during the irritable stage.

exercises.name: Light thumb-extension isometric
exercises.dose: Start with 5 holds of 10 seconds, building toward 5 holds of 20 seconds; rest about 60 seconds between holds
exercises.frequency: Once daily after Stage 1 is tolerated
exercises.how: Place the hand on its small-finger side with the wrist neutral and thumb in line with the forearm. Place a finger from the other hand against the back of the thumb. Gently attempt to lift the thumb while the other hand prevents movement. Begin at about 20 to 30 percent effort.
exercises.easier: Use five-second holds and very light pressure.
exercises.harder: Build the hold to 20 seconds, then increase toward moderate effort. Do not use maximal effort.

exercises.name: Slow thumb extension with light resistance
exercises.frequency: Every other day, beginning in Stage 3
exercises.how: Place a very light elastic loop around the fingers and thumb. Keep the wrist neutral. Slowly move the thumb away from the palm, pause briefly, then return over two to three seconds.
exercises.easier: Perform the movement without resistance.
exercises.harder: Reach 10 controlled repetitions before using a slightly firmer band. Do not add resistance when radial wrist pain increases.

exercises.name: Neutral-wrist functional hold
exercises.frequency: 3 days per week, beginning in Stage 3
exercises.how: Hold a light cup or similar object using the whole hand while keeping the wrist neutral. The task should remain easy enough to perform without compensating or gripping tightly.
exercises.easier: Use an empty plastic cup or hold with both hands.
exercises.harder: Add time first, then a small amount of weight. Progress one variable at a time.

responseIntro: Start with the first two movements. Add loading only when resting pain and irritability are improving. Do not repeatedly use the Finkelstein or Eichhoff maneuver as a stretch; provoking a diagnostic position is not a required rehabilitation exercise.
green: Motion is pain free or produces only very mild discomfort, technique remains relaxed, and symptoms return to baseline by the next morning.
yellow: Pain becomes sharp, exceeds about 2 to 3 out of 10, increases with each repetition, or remains worse the next morning. Reduce effort, range, repetitions, or task exposure.
red: Stop and arrange assessment for rapidly increasing swelling, redness, heat, new numbness, sudden weakness, triggering, deformity, or severe pain after trauma.

progression.title: Stage 1: calm and maintain motion
progression.text: Modify provoking tasks, use a comfortable orthosis selectively, and perform pain-free thumb and wrist motion. Do not strengthen through an irritable flare.

progression.title: Stage 2: introduce isometric load
progression.text: Add light thumb-extension isometrics. Build hold duration before effort. The exercise should not create a sustained increase in thumb-side wrist pain.

progression.title: Stage 3: restore dynamic capacity
progression.text: Add slow thumb extension with a light elastic and neutral-wrist functional holds when the earlier stage remains stable.

progression.title: Stage 4: return to specific demands
progression.text: Gradually restore lifting, gripping, infant care, racquet use, gym work, instrument playing, or occupational tasks. Increase duration, repetitions, or load one at a time.

readyItems: Resting pain and swelling are stable or improving.
Light thumb and wrist motion does not produce sharp pain.
The current stage has been tolerated for several sessions.
Symptoms return to baseline by the following morning.
Five light isometric holds can be completed without increasing pain.
Light daily tasks can be performed with a neutral wrist.
evaluation: Schedule an evaluation if symptoms are substantial, the diagnosis is uncertain, function worsens, the brace causes pressure or numbness, or there is no clear improvement after two to four weeks. Persistent confirmed De Quervain tenosynovitis merits discussion of clinician-directed options because exercise alone has limited supporting evidence.

faqs.q: Are exercises proven to treat De Quervain tenosynovitis?
faqs.a: Not yet. Available exercise studies are small, low quality, and multimodal. Pain-free motion and thumb-extension isometrics appear feasible, but exercise has not been shown to be an effective stand-alone treatment.

faqs.q: Should I stretch into the Finkelstein position?
faqs.a: No. Repeatedly forcing the thumb into the palm while deviating the wrist can strongly provoke the involved compartment. A positive diagnostic maneuver is not automatically a useful stretch.

faqs.q: Does a brace help?
faqs.a: A thumb-spica orthosis may reduce provocative loading. Evidence is strongest when immobilization is combined with a clinician-delivered corticosteroid injection. Orthosis-only schedules are less certain, so comfort and response should guide a short self-management trial.

faqs.q: How should I try the brace before an injection?
faqs.a: Use a comfortable thumb-spica orthosis during clearly aggravating tasks and, if helpful, at night for one to two weeks. Continue light hand use within comfort. The brace should support the wrist and thumb without pressing on the painful area or causing numbness, color change, or skin injury.

faqs.q: Should I get an injection?
faqs.a: Network meta-analyses, with important certainty limitations, favored corticosteroid injection plus thumb-spica immobilization. Injection suitability, technique, risks, and alternatives should be discussed with a qualified clinician.

faqs.q: Can I keep lifting my baby?
faqs.a: Usually, but technique and total load may need modification. Keep the wrists neutral, lift with the palms or forearms when possible, use both arms, and avoid repeatedly lifting with the thumbs spread and wrists angled toward the small-finger side.

faqs.q: What about massage, ultrasound, or scraping?
faqs.a: High-quality evidence for these treatments is limited. They should not displace diagnosis, activity modification, an appropriate orthosis, or discussion of better-supported medical options.
